text:
Alberta Court of
Queen's Bench

R. v. Tremblay

Date: 2000-08-03

E.K. White and S.P. MacKenzie, for the
Crown;

J.J. Markey, for the defence.

(Action No. 9901-0562-C2)

August 3, 2000.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Brooker
J.: — Judgment dated
December 17, 1999, Jean Guy Tremblay was convicted of six offences in relation
to two complainants, Tamarah Hallson and Tamara Monilaws [see
1999 ABQB 981 (CanLII)
, 257 A.R. 251].
Regarding Monilaws, Tremblay's convictions include assault causing bodily harm,
criminal harassment, and unlawful confinement. The offences involving Hallson
include uttering threats, common assault, and unlawful confinement.

[
2
]

In relation to those offences, the Crown brings
the current application to have Jean Guy Tremblay declared a dangerous offender
pursuant to
s. 753
of the
Criminal Code of
Canada
.

[
3
]

In the alternative, the Crown applies to have
Tremblay designated as a long-term offender pursuant to s. 753(5).

FACTS

[
4
]

A number of witnesses were called at the trial
of this matter and during the subject application to testify about their involvement
with Tremblay. For the most part I have accepted the evidence given by those
witnesses, most of which went largely unchallenged. What follows is a
chronology of the relevant facts as I have found them. It should be noted that
although I have considered all of the evidence, I have provided only a brief
summary for the purposes of this Judgment.

[
5
]

A review of the evidence that is relevant to
this application must begin with the testimony of Tremblay's mother, Estelle Lalonde.

[
6
]

Lalonde testified that she has two children, her
son, Jean Guy Tremblay, born December 14, 1963 and a daughter, born November 4, 1962. Lalonde and Tremblay's
father, whom she described as a "drunkard", are no longer married.

[
7
]

Lalonde testified that Tremblay suffered from
relatively significant health problems as a child. She also testified that he
demonstrated social difficulties at a very early age and was generally lonely
as a child.

[
8
]

When Tremblay was approximately four years old, Lalonde
returned to the workforce and he and his sister were sent to a private home for
childcare. The nature of this child-care was such that Tremblay and his sister
only returned home on the weekends and stayed with the private caregivers
during the week. This situation continued until Tremblay was approximately
eight or nine years of age. Lalonde testified that she had to switch care homes
on four or five occasions because her son would drive the caregivers to their
"wits end".

[
9
]

At age 13 Tremblay began to run away from home. Lalonde
testified that upon asking the state for assistance, Tremblay was placed with
an agency that looked after youth - "une famille d'accueil". Tremblay
remained within that system until he was 18.

[
10
]

Tremblay also had difficulty at school from an
early age. According to Lalonde he had to repeat grades "one, two and
three. And Secondary School one and two". By age eight or nine Tremblay
was skipping school and at 14 or 15 one school went so far as to expel him. He
quit school at age 16 but later returned to a residential school for children
with difficulties. Lalonde testified he did not go on to attend college or
university, but that he did commence a course in "tow truck business"
which he did not complete.

[
11
]

Lalonde testified that Tremblay was involved
with the criminal justice system by age 14. She stated that she lost contact
with her son after he reached age 18 and thereafter heard from him only
"when he was in trouble".

[
12
]

The next relevant chapter in Tremblay's life
concerns his well publicised relationship with Chantal Daigle. Daigle testified
that she met Tremblay at the end of November, 1988 at a store where she was
returning a broken answering machine. Daigle testified that Tremblay told her
that he was at the store assisting his half-brother. According to Lalonde,
Tremblay has no siblings other than his sister.

[
13
]

Shortly after their initial meeting Tremblay and
Daigle began a dating relationship. Tremblay told Daigle that he owned his own
company and that he had investments.

[
14
]

According to Daigle, Tremblay was "gentle
and nice" at the beginning of the relationship but he became increasingly
aggressive. She testified that he began to restrict her freedom and discouraged
her from spending time with her friends and family. Daigle described the
relationship as a "particularly gentle possession".

[
15
]

In February, 1989, Daigle received a telephone
call from a woman Tremblay referred to as his "half sister". She told
Daigle that her house, where Tremblay had been living, had been broken into and
she had been beaten by the thieves. Daigle felt that Tremblay could not
continue to live there in those circumstances and she invited him to move in
with her on a temporary basis.

[
16
]

Almost immediately after moving in, Tremblay
told Daigle that he wanted to get married and start a family. Daigle felt that
it was too early in the relationship to be considering such matters.
Nonetheless, she agreed to discontinue using birth control on the assumption
that it "normally takes months" to become pregnant. The following
month, in March, Daigle discovered that she was pregnant.

[
17
]

Tremblay repeatedly accused Daigle of being
unfaithful. She explained that he tried to be with her all the time in order to
prevent her from having "a lover". Tremblay would either attend at
her place of employment or he would call repeatedly. Daigle testified that she
felt as though she was in a "tightrope situation" wherein she had no
freedom. After becoming pregnant, she stated that she became "more his
property".

[
18
]

Tremblay began exhibiting violent behaviour
approximately one month after he and Daigle began living together. Daigle
recounted being grabbed by the arm and the throat, pushed, shaken, slapped on
the arm and dragged. In total there were approximately five incidents of
assaultive behaviour. Fortunately, she did not suffer any injuries.

[
19
]

In addition to the violence, Daigle recalled
Tremblay threatening to kick her out of the car and leave her along the side of
the road. He also threatened to destroy her property and harm her cat. She
testified that he would call her a "whore", tell her that she was
"unclean" and that she was worth "less than nothing".

[
20
]

Throughout the relationship Tremblay had a
series of short term jobs. Daigle, however, was responsible for paying the
bills and the rent.

[
21
]

In July 1989 after the couple had returned home
from a party, Tremblay accused Daigle of being "too social". When she
denied any such behaviour, Tremblay grabbed her by the throat and pushed her
down on the bed. After he released her she fled to the neighbours. She then
went to live with her parents in Chibougameau.

[
22
]

During the assaults which occurred after May 8, 1989 Tremblay was under a probation order
in relation to an earlier assault conviction. Daigle did not lay any complaints
with the police because she was too afraid.

[
23
]

Following the termination of her relationship
with Tremblay, Daigle suffered nightmares and lost her self-confidence. She
felt insecure to the point that she was afraid to leave the house and she
applied for a Firearms Acquisition Certificate. She testified that she did not
receive any counselling other than from her family and friends and that even at
the time of this application, over a decade since these incidents occurred, she
is more careful about where she goes and what she does.

[
24
]

In April of 1990 Tremblay met Martine Beaudoin.
The two became romantically involved in July, and in August Tremblay moved in
with Beaudoin and her 16 month old daughter.

[
25
]

Beaudoin was not called to give evidence.
Charges were laid against Tremblay as a result of his conduct during his
relationship with Beaudoin. The transcripts and the Judgment which resulted
from the trial of these charges were entered as exhibits at this hearing. That
evidence indicates that over a period of three days in October 1990, Tremblay
physically assaulted Beaudoin on a number of occasions, including pushing her,
throwing her, slapping her, grabbing her and choking her. Beaudoin suffered
cuts to her mouth and red marks over her jaw. Tremblay also made threats to
hurt her again, and to kill her if she left him. He also threatened to kill
himself if she left him.

[
26
]

The transcripts from the Beaudoin trial also
indicate that Tremblay tried to disallow Beaudoin from contacting her family
and that he accused her of being unfaithful.

[
27
]

On October 12 Beaudoin's father called the
police and Tremblay was arrested. Beaudoin described her experience with
Tremblay as having been "terrorized".

[
28
]

When the matter went to trial, Tremblay denied
all of the incidents. He explained that Beaudoin's injuries were the result of
an accident.

[
29
]

Judge Dubreuil of the Quebec
Provincial Court, rejected Tremblay's version of
events and, on May 7, 1991, convicted him of two counts of assault and two
counts of uttering threats. Tremblay received a custodial sentence of six
months less one day and three years probation including terms that he have no
contact with Beaudoin or her family.

[
30
]

On June 27, 1991, Tremblay was convicted of
assault causing bodily harm in relation to his friend's landlady. I do not
intend to review the facts of that offence in detail as they are not relevant
to these proceedings. What is relevant is that the events supporting that
conviction occurred on February 7, 1991, while Tremblay was on release in
relation to the charges concerning Beaudoin. Tremblay was sentenced to six
months custody, consecutive to the term he was serving in relation to the Beaudoin
convictions together with three years probation. Tremblay remained in custody
from May 7, 1991 to January 4,
1992.

[
31
]

In July of 1992, Tremblay moved from Montreal to Calgary.

[
32
]

Bette Jean (B.J.) Fontana was called by the Crown to give evidence at trial but not at this
application. However, her trial testimony is admissible as all of the
transcripts from the trial were entered as an exhibit in these proceedings.

[
33
]

In mid-January 1994, Tremblay met Fontana at a bar. Tremblay told her that he
was a well-known professional hockey player with the Toronto Maple Leafs. That
evening Fontana gave Tremblay
her phone number and over the next three or four weeks he called her on a daily
basis.

[
34
]

Approximately one month after their initial
meeting, Tremblay told Fontana
that he was having some difficulties with his current roommate and asked if
could move in with her. Believing that he was down on his luck, she agreed.

[
35
]

After Tremblay moved in with Fontana he insisted on driving her to work
despite the fact that her place of employment was only two blocks away. He
began to call her frequently at work and he isolated her from her friends. He
told her that her friends were using her and that he preferred that they not be
invited over to their apartment.

[
36
]

In March 1994, while Tremblay was living with Fontana, he met Lucia Cariolato. Cariolato
was called as a witness both at trial and during the course of this
application.

[
37
]

Cariolato met Tremblay through her common law
partner who was a friend of Tremblay's. Cariolato's common law partner was
physically abusive towards her and when Tremblay discovered this he actively
counselled her to leave the relationship, telling her that she should not be
treated in that manner.

[
38
]

At the beginning of April 1994, Cariolato left
her common law relationship and moved in with her aunt. Thereafter she began a
dating relationship with Tremblay and two weeks later, at Tremblay's
invitation, Cariolato moved in with him and Fontana.

[
39
]

By mid-May of 1994, Cariolato discovered that
she was pregnant with Tremblay's child. Thereafter Tremblay began to assert
increasing control over her. He drove her to work, showed up at her place of
employment while she was working and picked her up at the end of the day. He
forced her to eat, told her what to wear and insisted that she leave the door
unlocked when she was bathing. On the odd occasion that he worked, he would
force Cariolato to go with him and stay throughout the duration of his shift.

[
40
]

At the beginning of June 1994, Tremblay, Fontana and Cariolato moved out of their
apartment and into a duplex. Fontana testified that after they moved Tremblay insisted that she not give
out her new phone number to her friends.

[
41
]

At the end of June, Fontana, who had been paying Tremblay's share of the rent, told him that
she would have to move out if he did not start paying his own share of the
rent. Tremblay became enraged and told her that if she left he would find her
no matter where she went and "fix it so that [she] would not be able to
walk". Fontana began to
fear for her safety.

[
42
]

On another occasion Tremblay became enraged and
knocked a bottle of water out of Fontana's hand, sending it flying across the room. He also threw a box of
cheques at her, narrowly missing her face. He would say that if she did not do
or say something that he wanted her to, he would "hammer" her. She
compared the time that she spent living with Tremblay in the duplex to
"walking on egg shells".

[
43
]

On July 16, 1994, after asking Tremblay to
turn down the stereo, Tremblay kicked her in her calf area, shoved her shoulder
causing her to fall into a wall, and again threatened to "hammer"
her.

[
44
]

On July 20, Tremblay pushed Fontana in the chest with both hands
causing her glasses to fall partially off her face. He struck her twice over
her ear with an open, cupped hand and threatened to hit her in the face. Fontana suffered no serious injuries as a
result of these assaults.

[
45
]

On July 21, 1994, Fontana contacted the police and Tremblay was charged with and subsequently
convicted of assault.

[
46
]

Tremblay was also violent towards Cariolato. In
July of 1994, while she was pregnant, Tremblay hit Cariolato across the stomach
with his arm. Although the blow left no marks, she testified that she felt sick
for about an hour after being struck.

[
47
]

In September 1994, Tremblay hit Cariolato on the
back of the head causing her to spill the soup that she was eating. During that
same month he grabbed her by the hair because she was not looking at him while
he was talking to her.

[
48
]

Cariolato left the relationship in October 1994.
She testified that she had planned to leave Tremblay for some time but needed
to build up his trust to get him to leave her alone long enough that she could
make her escape. Finally, while he was away at a job interview, she moved out
of their townhouse. Later, fearful that Tremblay might find her, she moved out
of the province. No charges were brought in relation to any of the incidents
involving Cariolato.

[
49
]

During the various assaults on Fontana and Cariolato, Tremblay was on probation
for the 1991 assault causing bodily harm conviction and the Beaudoin
convictions. After July 1994, he was also on judicial interim release in
relation to the Fontana charge.

[
50
]

Tremblay met Arlene Nissen in September 1994,
when he was hired to work at a glass business that she and her husband
operated. In October 1994, shortly after Tremblay began working for the couple,
Nissen discovered Tremblay in the garage with the door shut and the exhaust
running. As a result, the Nissens invited Tremblay to live with them until he
was able to get back on his feet. Although Tremblay only worked in the glass
business for a period of one or two weeks, he resided with the Nissen family
for approximately six months. During that period, Tremblay continued to talk
about ending his life and made what appeared to be two more suicide attempts.

[
51
]

Nissen testified that at Tremblay's invitation,
she attended approximately five counselling sessions with him at the end of
1994 or the beginning of 1995. Tremblay attended the counselling of his own
volition, however, he quit attending counselling after his counsellor moved
away.

[
52
]

In late December 1994, Graeme MacDonald, a
probation officer, was contacted to prepare a pre-sentence report for the Fontana conviction. MacDonald testified
that during his interview Tremblay told him that he had played 132 NHL games
with the Toronto Maple Leafs, that he was a blackbelt in hap-ki-do and that he
had a Masters Degree in computer programming from Notre
Dame University in Saskatchewan. None of those statements are
true.

[
53
]

Ultimately, MacDonald recommended that Tremblay
be considered for probation following a term of incarceration.

[
54
]

Tremblay was convicted of the Fontana assault in March 1995, and was
initially sentenced to a one year custodial term and two years probation, which
included conditions that he undergo treatment and that he not enter any
common-law relationships.

[
55
]

Tremblay was released from custody on March 25,
1995 on appeal bail. During his period of incarceration he was enrolled in an
anger management course. There is no indication that the program was
successfully completed.

[
56
]

Stephanie Nikiforuk was called as a Crown
witness at trial. She met Tremblay in September 1995, when she and a friend
were at a local night club. Tremblay told Nikiforuk that he was a pilot with
Delta Airlines and that he was based out of Houston. He explained that he rented a room in North East Calgary because
he flew to Calgary often.

[
57
]

Thereafter the two began a dating relationship.
One or two weeks into the relationship Nikiforuk's grandfather died and she had
to travel to Saskatchewan for
the funeral. Tremblay asked if he could go with her. When she refused he became
"very upset, very angry". He later told her that he had followed her
to Red Deer in order to ensure
that she was actually going to Saskatchewan.

[
58
]

Nikiforuk asked Tremblay to look after her cat
while she was away and she gave him a spare set of keys to her house. He then
began to reside at her apartment.

[
59
]

Approximately three weeks after Nikiforuk met
Tremblay he told her to refer to him as her husband. She was uncomfortable with
the fact that he never left her apartment and when she began to notice his
belongings showing up in her apartment, an argument ensued.

[
60
]

That night Tremblay would not let Nikiforuk go to
sleep until the argument was settled. The next day he would not let her go to
work and he threatened to kill himself if she left. Nikiforuk stayed home from
work that day.

[
61
]

Eventually Tremblay would not let Nikiforuk see
her mother. He also discouraged her from seeing her friends by telling her that
they were all using her. He began to tell her what to wear. If she did not
comply, he would threaten her. He started to do the cooking and he would insist
that she ate what he made when he made it.

[
62
]

Tremblay insisted on driving Nikiforuk to work,
visiting her during her breaks and picking her up at the end of the day. If she
was late leaving work he would become angry and demand to know why she was
late, to whom she had been talking and what she had been doing. She testified
that he would call her at work eight to ten times per day. When she tried to
hang up, he would threaten to attend at her place of work. On at least one
occasion he threatened to"beat [her] face".

[
63
]

Tremblay also threatened to kill Nikiforuk's cat,
to break her wrists and fingers, to choke her to the point of unconsciousness
and to"punch her head in". He also commented that he knew where her
mother lived. On one occasion he punched a hole in the wall.

[
64
]

Often, when Nikiforuk tried to leave the room,
he would restrain her by the wrists. Eventually she started to wear
long-sleeved shirts so that no one would notice the bruising. If she needed to
go to the store he would not let her go unaccompanied. Generally, she was
"not to leave the apartment alone".

[
65
]

When Tremblay told Nikiforuk to stop using birth
control pills she complied with his request because she was afraid of him.

[
66
]

During an argument on or about December 9, 1995, Tremblay ran towards Nikiforuk
and punched her in the chest, knocking her onto the bed. He then held her down
by her wrists. As a result of that incident Nikiforuk suffered a bruise to her
chest.

[
67
]

Two days later Nikiforuk contacted the police.
She left her apartment and did not return until Tremblay was in custody. He was
charged with two counts of assault causing bodily harm. Those charges were
eventually reduced on appeal to two counts of common assault. The assaults
against Nikiforuk occurred while he was on appeal bail in relation to the Fontana charge.

[
68
]

Tremblay was remanded in custody pending trial
on the Nikiforuk charges on December 12, 1995. On February 9, 1996 he was sentenced to two
years consecutive, however that sentence was reduced to five months following
his appeal. His sentence in relation to the Fontana charge was also reduced on appeal to a term of six months. While
incarcerated, Tremblay was involved in a Behaviour Management Program. He was
unable to complete the program because he was moved into administrative
segregation. Tremblay was released from custody on all of those charges on
December 24, 1996.

[
69
]

On January 16, 1997, Tremblay's probation
officer, Keith Kloster, directed that he attend for treatment at the Peter Lougheed
Centre. Tremblay finally attended the Centre almost six and one half months
later on August 1, 1997. On his first visit he advised the social worker, David
Mackrory, that he would not be returning because he did not think he required
any counselling or treatment and because he had a bad experience at another
hospital in the past. Mackrory suggested that Tremblay pursue community based
treatment. He never did.

[
70
]

Despite Tremblay's failure to comply with his
Probation Order, no breach charges were laid.

[
71
]

In late September 1997, Tremblay met Tamarah Hallson,
one of the victims in relation to the current offences. The evidence in this
regard is more fully set out in my Judgment dated December 17, 1999. I will summarize it here
for the sake of convenience.

[
72
]

Hallson met Tremblay at the Fifth Avenue Auto Haus
where Hallson was working as a salesperson. At the time Hallson was looking for
cheaper accommodations and Tremblay suggested that she move into the vacant
room in his basement suite. Hallson agreed.

[
73
]

Once Hallson and Tremblay were roommates he
became extremely controlling. He would tell Hallson where to sit, when to eat,
when she was supposed to be at home, when she could go to sleep, what she had
to wear, and whether she was allowed to leave the house. He told her what time
she was to be home and, on occasion, he told her that if she did not return by
a specified time she would not be allowed to go to work the following day.

[
74
]

Hallson was often late for work because she
would have to negotiate with Tremblay to let her leave the house. She testified
that on seven or eight occasions Tremblay pushed her to the floor when she
disobeyed his instructions. When she tried to get up, Tremblay would push her
down again. On other occasions Tremblay would simply stand in front of the
door.

[
75
]

Approximately one week after they began living
together, Hallson tried to "sneak out" of the house. She made it as
far as her car when she saw Tremblay coming towards her. She locked the door
and tried to get the car started. Tremblay told her to get out of the car and
when she refused, he broke her car window with his fist, took the keys out of
the ignition and said "forget it, get back in the house".

[
76
]

Hallson tried to "make a run for it" a
few times. On one such occasion, she ran up the stairs towards the door.
Tremblay grabbed her by the back of her coat and pulled her halfway back down the
stairs. She received a bruise on her right leg and a bruise on her lower back
or buttock area as a result of that incident.

[
77
]

On another occasion Tremblay dragged Hallson
into the kitchen causing her to receive a bruise on her left leg. His behaviour
aggravated old injuries to her back which she had received in a motor vehicle
accident.

[
78
]

Tremblay threatened Hallson, saying things such
as: "I will … kill you";"You've got no one here and there's no
one here to help you, so you leave when I say"; "if you were to go
missing, no one would notice and no one would care." Hallson testified
that she took the threats seriously and believed that Tremblay would kill her.

[
79
]

With the assistance of the police and some of
her colleagues at the Auto Haus, Hallson moved out on October 17, 1997.
Tremblay's involvement with Hallson resulted in three of the convictions which
are the subject of this application - one count each of common assault,
uttering threats and unlawful confinement.

[
80
]

On or about November 13, 1998, Tamara Monilaws met
Tremblay at a local nightclub. Monilaws is the victim in relation to three of
the convictions from the trial of this matter, specifically one count each of
unlawful confinement assault causing bodily harm and criminal harassment. The
specific details of the offences are included in the trial Judgment dated
December 17, 1999. I have included a brief summary of my findings here for ease
of reference.

[
81
]

When Monilaws met Tremblay he introduced himself
as Giovanni Hachuk and told her that he was a professional hockey player. Monilaws
testified that after their initial meeting she and Tremblay "hit it
off" and they became romantically involved.

[
82
]

Two weeks later, at the end of November or the
beginning of December, Tremblay moved in with Monilaws and her two year old
son. Tremblay told Monilaws that he had nowhere else to live because he and his
hockey trainer were not getting along and because he had broken his hand and
his hockey career was over. Although Monilaws consented to Tremblay moving in,
she testified that she thought that it was only a temporary arrangement.

[
83
]

Monilaws' evidence was that after Tremblay moved in he
began to control her life. She stated that Tremblay did all of the cooking and
would became angry if she or her son did not finish everything on their plates.
She testified further that he dictated what they would watch on television, and
that Tremblay would often insist on watching television loudly at night with
the volume so high that she was unable to sleep. He prohibited her from showering
alone and would insist on washing her. He took her house and car keys and insisted
on driving her to and from work. When she had to take a taxi to work, Tremblay
told her that he called the cab company to make sure she actually did take the
cab to work. She recounted how Tremblay insisted that they get a new phone
number and then forbade Monilaws from giving the new phone number to anyone
other than her parents and her employer.

[
84
]

A few weeks after they began living together, Tremblay began to verbally
threaten and physically abuse Monilaws. Tremblay's conviction for assault
causing bodily harm in relation to Monilaws included over twenty separate
incidents of violence. The most serious incidents involved Tremblay choking her
to the point of unconsciousness, and banging her head against cement surfaces. Monilaws
suffered a variety of injuries as a result of the abuse including extensive
bruising and a damaged thumb. She testified that she was subjected to some form
of violence approximately twice a week.

[
85
]

During the course of their three and a half month common law
relationship Monilaws was rarely allowed to leave the house without Tremblay.
On one occasion he dragged her back into the house in order to continue a
particularly severe beating. When he permitted her to go to work he insisted on
driving her there and picking her up. Throughout the workday, Tremblay would
call her persistently. When she was not available to take his calls he would
either attend at her office or leave threatening voice mail messages.

[
86
]

Tremblay's relationship with Monilaws ended on or about March 19, 1999, when the couple attended at an appointment with a counsellor, Mr. Martin Michnick.
Tremblay had arranged for the appointment so that the counsellor could teach Monilaws
how to act so that she would not set him off.

OPINION EVIDENCE

[
87
]

Both the Crown and the Defence called expert evidence in the course of
these proceedings. The Crown called one psychiatrist, Dr. Hashman, and two
psychologists, Drs. Nesca and Dutton. The Defence called Drs. Weston and
Baillie, a psychiatrist and psychologist, respectively.

[
88
]

The Alberta Court of Appeal in
R. v. Neve (L.C.)
(1999),
1999 ABCA 206 (CanLII)
, 237 A.R.
201;
197 W.A.C. 201
; 137 C.C.C.(3d) 97; 71 Alta. L.R.(3d) 92 (C.A.), instructs
