prohibitions on access to adult heterosexual relationships - with a therapist
who understands a relapse prevention model [the model being developed by
Doctors Hare and West], and with Mr. Tremblay's compliance with treatment, that
there is a window of possibility for treatment to be effective."

[
154
]

While Dr. Baillie is of the opinion that Tremblay's
treatment must begin with a custodial sentence, he is also of the opinion that
treatment must continue once Tremblay is released into the community. According
to Dr. Baillie the opportunities for Tremblay to get community based treatment
are "quite good". Specifically, he is of the opinion that treatment
through Parole Board funded contractors and FAOS would be adequate. Were
Tremblay to receive an indeterminate sentence Dr. Baillie believed, based on
his previous experience, that the corrections system would view him as a low
priority in terms of providing therapy.

APPLICATION OF R. v. NEVE

[
155
]

In relation to the dangerous offender
application the Crown relies on s. 753(1)(a)(i) and (ii):

" (i) a pattern of repetitive
behaviour by the offender, of which the offence for which he or she has been
convicted forms a part, showing a failure to restrain his or her behaviour and
a likelihood of causing death or injury to other persons, or inflicting severe
psychological damage on other persons, through failure in the future to
restrain his or her behaviour; or

"(ii) a pattern of persistent
aggressive behaviour by the offender, of which the offence for which he or she
has been convicted forms a part, showing a substantial degree of indifference
on the part of the offender respecting the reasonably foreseeable consequences
to other persons of his or her behaviour."

[
156
]

The Crown argued strenuously that the only
issues which need to be considered on a dangerous offender application concern
whether or not the offender satisfies the statutory criteria set out at
s. 753
.
It took the position that the final threshold set out in
Neve
,
residual
discretion, is no longer applicable in light of the amendments to the dangerous
offender provisions that came into force on August 1, 1997. I reject that argument.

[
157
]

In Neve the Court provided an analysis of the
statutory criteria under
s. 753
and determined that where the offender meets
those criteria the sentencing court must go on to consider whether the
offender, in all of the circumstances, falls within that small group of
offenders targeted by the legislation. Where that question is answered in the
negative, the Court found that it is appropriate for the trial judge to
exercise his or her discretion to decline to make the designation. At
paragraphs 227 and 228, the Court of Appeal stated:

"We now turn our attention to the
last step in the dangerous offender analysis. As noted earlier, even if a court
should find that all the statutory criteria for designating someone a dangerous
offender have been met, there remains in the sentencing judge a discretion
whether to make the designation …

"The existence of this final review,
giving to the sentencing judge an overriding discretion, indeed a duty, to
decide whether to designate a person as dangerous, recognizes that the
statutory criteria, if applied literally, could sometimes lead to an unjust
result. It is precisely because this legislation is not applied on the basis of
rigid classifications but accepted standards of rationality and proportionality
that
Charter
challenges have failed. Indeed, it is the existence of the
various layers of judicial discretion, including this layer at the very end,
which, in part, shield the dangerous offender proceedings from
Charter
challenges
…"

[
158
]

Arguing that the amendments to the
Code
have
effectively eliminated this final threshold, the Crown relied on the Ontario
Court of Appeal's decision in
R. v. Moore
(1985),
1985 CanLII 5991 (ON CA)
, 7 O.A.C. 33;
1985 CanLII 1971 (ON CA)
, 16
C.C.C.(3d) 328 (C.A.). At the time of that decision the relevant legislation
read in part as follows:

"688. Where, upon an application …
it is established to the satisfaction of the court

(a) that the
offence for which the offender has been convicted is a serious personal injury
offence … and the offender constitutes a threat to the life, safety or physical
or mental well being of other persons on the basis of evidence establishing

(i) a pattern
of repetitive behaviour … showing a failure to restrain his behaviour and a
likelihood of his causing death or injury … through failure in the future to
restrain his behaviour, …

(ii) a pattern
of persistent aggressive behaviour … showing a substantial degree of
indifference … as to the reasonably foreseeable consequences …, or

(iii) any
behaviour by the offender … that is of such a brutal nature … that his
behaviour in the future is unlikely to be inhibited by normal standards.

. . . . .

"The court
may
find the
offender to be a dangerous offender and
may
thereupon impose a sentence
of detention in a penitentiary for an indeterminate period, in lieu of any
other sentence that might be imposed for the offence for which the offender has
been convicted." (emphasis added)

[
159
]

In
Moore

the Court held that the first
"may" in s. 688 conferred a power, as opposed to a discretion. In
that regard the Ontario Court of Appeal relied on the reasons of Clement, J.A.,
in
R. v. Carleton,
1981 ABCA 220 (CanLII)
, [1981] 6 W.W.R. 148; 32 A.R. 181; 69 C.C.C.(2d) 1; 23
C.R.(3d) 129 (C.A.), affd.

1983 CanLII 157 (SCC)
, [1983] 2 S.C.R. 58; 52 N.R. 293;
47 A.R. 160
, where he concluded that the first
"may" was imperative in the sense that once the case is proven the
court must exercise the power to find the offender a dangerous offender.

[
160
]

Although the decision of the Alberta Court of
Appeal in
Carleton
was upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada (
1983 CanLII 157 (SCC)
, [1983] 2
S.C.R.58), the majority of the seven judge panel concurred with the decision of
McGillivray, C.J.A., who found it unnecessary to decide whether the first
"may" is imperative. Moreover, in the subsequent decision of the
Supreme Court in
R. v. Lyons,
1987 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 309; 80 N.R. 161; 82
N.S.R.(2d) 271; 207 A.P.R. 271; 37 C.C.C. (3d) 1; 61 C.R.(3d) 1; 44 D.L.R.(4th)
193, the majority, per La Forest, J., expressly concluded that there was a
discretion in the court to decline to make the designation. At page 361
[S.C.R.] La Forest, J., stated:

"Finally, it is not insignificant
that … the judge at such a hearing does retain a discretion whether or not to
impose the designation or indeterminate sentence, or both."

[
161
]

In
Neve
,
the Court relied on
Lyons

and
implied that
Carleton
and
Moore
were no longer good law to the
extent that they held that there was no residual discretion. At paragraph 239
the Court stated:

"Contrary to earlier views, the
Supreme Court also confirmed in
Lyons
,
supra, that the sentencing judge does
retain a discretion to decline to designate someone a dangerous offender even
though all the statutory criteria have been met."

[
162
]

In any event, it is clear that the Court
declined to adopt the reasoning in
Carleton
and
Moore
in relation
to the issue of residual discretion and instead followed the majority decision
of the Supreme Court in
Lyons
.

[
163
]

The Crown, however, took the position that La
Forest, J.'s comments in
Lyons
,
which the Court in
Neve
relied
on to find residual discretion, were obiter dictum. In support of its position the
Crown cited
R. v. R.C.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 11059 (NL CA)
, 145 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 271; 453 A.P.R.
271 (Nfld. C.A.), where the
Newfoundland Court of Appeal found that La Forest, J.'s statement was not the
ratio decidendi of the case.

[
164
]

With respect, I cannot conclude that La Forest,
J.'s comments in
Lyons

were obiter dictum. In that decision
the Supreme Court considered whether the dangerous offender provisions
contravened
ss. 7
,
9
,
11
, or
12
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
.
While the existence of a residual discretion was not a singularly
important consideration in the Court's decision to uphold the legislation, the
existence of the discretion was considered an important component of "a
tailored set of criteria" which ensured that the legislation met the requisite
standards of rationality and proportionality.

[
165
]

Although
Lyons
was not decided in the
context of the present legislation, given the more severe consequences now
flowing from a dangerous offender designation as a result of the 1997
amendments (automatic indeterminate sentences and the time until the offender's
first review increased from three to seven years) it seems only logical that
the element of discretion would assume greater importance. In other words, if
the element of discretion was necessary to the constitutionality of the
provisions prior to the 1997 amendments, surely that discretion must be even
more necessary in light of the current penal consequences.

[
166
]

In any event, although
Neve
was
considered on the basis of the old legislation, it is clear throughout the
Judgment that the Court of Appeal was cognizant of the 1997 amendments. Mindful
of the new provisions, the Court undertook a detailed analysis of dangerous
offender proceedings and laid out a virtual template for trial judges to follow
in considering dangerous offender applications. Had our Court of Appeal
intended the detailed procedure it prescribed in
Neve

to apply only to
the dangerous offender provisions as they existed prior to the 1997 amendments,
such that the methodology provided (including the final threshold), would be of
little or no precedential value, one would have expected some discussion to
that effect.

[
167
]

Further, the rationale used in support of the
analysis adopted by the Court in
Neve

is equally applicable and sound in
relation to the wording of the amended provisions. That factor, in my view,
also dictates against the position taken by the Crown.

[
168
]

Finally, the existence of a residual discretion
is consistent with the current legislation in view of accepted principles of
statutory interpretation and, more specifically,
s. 11
of the
Interpretation
Act,
R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, which states:

"11. The expression 'shall' is to be
construed as imperative and the expression 'may' as permissive."

[
169
]

In my view, if Parliament had intended the
designation of dangerous offender to follow automatically once the statutory
prerequisites were satisfied it would have amended the first "may" to
"shall". Parliament can be presumed to have been aware that the
Supreme Court in
Lyons

had interpreted the legislation to have
included a residual discretion. If that interpretation was not consonant with
Parliament's intent one would have expected the 1997 amendments to have changed
the first "may" to "shall". This seems particularly clear
given that it amended the second "may" to "shall" in order
to eliminate the discretion to impose an indeterminate sentence.

[
170
]

This interpretation is consistent with the view
taken by Knazan, J., of the Ontario Court of Justice in
R. v. M.B.,

[2000] O.J. No. 2135 (Sup. Ct.)
.
There the Court accepted the argument that the first "may" did confer
a discretion on the sentencing judge. At paragraph 143 Knazan, J., stated:

"I start from the premise that
Parliament meant 'may' when it said 'may' in s. 753 as it applies in this case,
and that the Supreme Court of Canada had a reason for so interpreting the
section and so clearly stating that the court has the discretion not to declare
an offender to be a dangerous offender even if he meets the criteria."

[
171
]

In that case it was unclear whether the offences
occurred prior to the coming into force of the 1997 amendments. However, at
paragraph 285 the Court specifically looked at the effect of those amendments
and maintained its finding with respect to the existence of a discretion at the
designation stage.

[
172
]

For these reasons I reject the Crown's argument
and conclude that where an offender satisfies the statutory criteria set out at
s. 753, the Court has a discretion to decline to designate that offender as a
dangerous offender.

ISSUES

[
173
]

Having found that the judicial discretion
analysis in
Neve

continues to apply despite the 1997 amendments to the
Criminal
Code

and recognizing that that decision is binding on me, I will proceed
with my analysis in accordance with
Neve.
Accordingly, I find that the
issues in the present application are as follows:

1. Do any of the
offences for which Tremblay has been convicted constitute a "serious
personal injury offence"?

2. Has it been
established that Tremblay constitutes a threat to the life, safety or physical
or mental well being of other persons on the basis of evidence of his past
behaviour as set out in any one of the three prescribed thresholds under s.
753(1)(a)?

3. If the answers to
the above questions are "yes", is a dangerous offender designation
appropriate in all of the circumstances?

4. If a dangerous
offender designation is inappropriate should Tremblay be designated as a
long-term offender in accordance with s. 753.1?

ANALYSIS

1. Do any of the
offences for which Tremblay has been convicted constitute a "serious
personal injury offence"?

[
174
]

Section 752(a) of the
Code
provides the
definition of serious personal injury offence which is relevant to this
application:

'"serious personal injury offence'
means

(a) an
indictable offence … involving

(i) the use or
attempted use of violence against another person, or

(ii) conduct
endangering or likely to endanger the life or safety of another person or
inflicting or likely to inflict severe psychological damage upon another
person,

and for which the offender may be
sentenced to imprisonment for ten years or more, …"

[
175
]

According to
Neve
,
in order to constitute
a serious personal injury offence, the violence or attempted violence, as
contemplated by s. 752(a)(i), or endangerment, as set out in s. 752(a)(ii),
must be objectively serious. Moreover, in order to find
"endangerment" there must exist a likelihood of material harm,
whether physical or psychological.

[
176
]

The Crown submits that of Tremblay's six current
convictions, the assault causing bodily harm in relation to Monilaws and both
the unlawful confinement convictions constitute serious personal injury
offences.

[
177
]

Pursuant to s. 267 of the
Code,
a person
convicted of assault causing bodily harm may be liable to a term of
imprisonment of up to 10 years.

[
178
]

The facts supporting the assault causing bodily
harm conviction include over 20 separate incidents of violence against Monilaws.
The number, nature and frequency of the assaults convince me beyond a
reasonable doubt that the threshold of objective seriousness is met, both in
terms of violence under s. 752(a)(i) and in terms of endangerment under s.
752(a)(ii).

[
179
]

Monilaws sustained numerous injuries from the
assaults, both physically and psychologically. Physically the injuries included
an injury to her thumb which may be permanent. Her psychological injuries
include depression, anxiety, nightmares, flashbacks and difficulty sleeping.
Given the extent of the abuse that she endured it would be surprising if some
degree of psychological injury had not resulted. On the basis of the above evidence
I am satisfied that not only was there "a likelihood of material physical
or psychological harm" as required by
Neve
,
but that that harm was
realized.

[
180
]

In the result I find that the Crown has
established that Tremblay has been convicted of an offence that constitutes a
serious personal injury offence.

[
181
]

Once a single predicate offence is found to be a
serious personal injury offence, the dangerous offender gate is open for all
purposes. Accordingly, I need not consider whether any of Tremblay's other
convictions constitute serious personal injury offences.

2. Has it been

established that
Tremblay
constitutes a threat to the life, safety or physical
or mental well-being of other persons on the basis of evidence of his past
behaviour as set out in any one of the three prescribed thresholds under s.
753(1)(a)?

[
182
]

The determination of whether Tremblay
constitutes a threat under s. 753(1)(a) requires that I undertake a two step
analysis:

a. Has the Crown
proven that the offender's past conduct meets one of the thresholds specified
in s. 753; and

b. Does the offender
constitute a threat in the nature contemplated by the section.

a) The Threshold Assessment

[
183
]

In this application the Crown is relying on the
thresholds outlined in s. 753(1)(a)(i) and (ii). In order to prove that either
of those thresholds are met the Crown must show that the offender's past
conduct constitutes one of the proscribed patterns in those subsections. The
required elements under s. 753(1)(a)(i) are:

1. that there is a
pattern of repetitive behaviour;

2. that the predicate
offence forms part of that pattern;

3. that the pattern
shows a failure by the offender to restrain his or her behaviour in the past;
and

4. that the pattern
shows a likelihood of death, injury or severe psychological damage to other
persons through failure to restrain his or her behaviour in the future.

[
184
]

The requisite elements of s. 753(1)(a)(ii) are:

1. a pattern of
persistent aggressive behaviour;

2. that the predicate
offence forms part of the pattern; and

3. that the pattern
shows a substantial degree of indifference by the offender respecting the
reasonably foreseeable consequences of his or her behaviour.

[
185
]

Three general areas of evidence will be
considered in determining whether the past conduct forms a pattern which falls
within the threshold requirements: the offender's past criminal acts, the
circumstances surrounding those acts and any extrinsic evidence relevant
thereto and expert evidence opining as to those criminal acts.

[
186
]

In order to find that there is a pattern for the
purposes of s. 753, the Court must only have regard to past criminal conduct.
That conduct may include uncharged criminal acts so long as they are proven
beyond a reasonable doubt. In the context of the current application I have
already found, following a voir dire during the course of this application,
that the Crown has proven the uncharged acts of assault against Daigle and Cariolato
beyond a reasonable doubt.

[
187
]

In order to form part of the pattern an offence
must involve some degree of violence or attempted violence, endangerment or
likely endangerment. Further, the criminal conduct must demonstrate persistence
in the sense of similarity, either in terms of the kind of offences or in terms
of result, having regard to the degree of violence or aggression threatened or
inflicted.

[
188
]

In the present case I have no hesitation in
finding beyond a reasonable doubt that Tremblay's previous criminal conduct
demonstrates a pattern of persistent criminal behaviour typified by violence
and endangerment towards women with whom he lives. Specifically, I find that
Tremblay's pattern consists of his criminal conduct towards Hallson (assault,
unlawful confinement, uttering threats), Monilaws (assault causing bodily harm,
criminal harassment, unlawful confinement.), Nikiforuk (assault), Cariolato
(assault), Fontana (assault), Daigle (assault) and Beaudoin (assault, uttering
threats).

[
189
]

I should note that I had previously found
following a voir dire that the Crown has also proven past criminal conduct in
relation to two other women, Joanne Olsen and Hope Fleming. However, I have
found that those acts do not form part of Tremblay's pattern and as a result I
have not considered that evidence in relation to this assessment.

[
190
]

Additionally, the Crown called evidence from one
of Tremblay's former landladies, Kari-Lynne Kelly. Although Tremblay's conduct
in relation to Kelly may also constitute uncharged criminal acts, Kelly was not
called during the voir dire held to determine what, if any, of the uncharged
criminal conduct was proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Further the Crown did
not argue that Kelly fell on the pattern scale. Thus, I have not considered her
evidence in relation to my analysis.

[
191
]

Why Tremblay's offences form a pattern becomes
even more apparent when one undertakes a contextual assessment of Tremblay's
criminal conduct and considers the surrounding circumstances in each case. In
every one of those instances, when Tremblay made contact with the victim, he
generally misrepresented himself as an individual of some means, for example as
a professional hockey player or an airline pilot. Shortly after meeting the
victim he would find a way to move in with them. Typically, Tremblay would
offer a hard luck story in order to elicit an invitation to move in: with
Daigle it was an alleged break-in at his non-existent half-sister's home where
he had been living, in Monilaws' case his imagined hockey career was at an end,
and with Fontana and Nikiforuk
he was having trouble with his roommates. Although not mentioned in her own
testimony, Cariolato reportedly told Dr. Dutton during her interview that
Tremblay represented to her that he had a large house in Quebec, that he spent lots of money and
that he played professional hockey. Hallson testified that Tremblay told her he
had recently been in a car accident. The Pre-sentence report authored by Jeff
Wood accurately described this manoeuvring as a "a repertoire of tragic
and grandiose stories" designed to lure women into a relationship.

[
192
]

In each case, after he had moved in with the
victim, Tremblay would assert increasing control over their lives. The tools
employed by Tremblay in asserting control over his victims also demonstrated
undeniable similarity. Examples of this are telling the victim what to wear,
what and when to eat, when she could and could not leave the house, when she
had to return home, isolating her from her friends and family, phoning her
repeatedly at work, insisting on driving her to work and picking her up,
threatening her family and/or herself, insisting that the bathroom door remain
open while bathing and keeping her awake at night.

[
193
]

Although the nature of the criminal conduct
which constitutes the pattern may not have been similar in degree in every
case, it was clearly similar in kind. Based on the evidence of those victims,
whose names are set out in paragraph 188 herein, I have no difficulty finding
that there existed some form of violence, attempted violence and endangerment
or likely endangerment in each case.

[
194
]

In addition to the above behavioural criteria,
the Crown must also prove, pursuant to s. 753(1)(a)(i) that Tremblay's pattern
demonstrates a future likelihood of injury or severe psychological damage to
others as a result of his failure to restrain his behaviour. Under s.
753(1)(a)(ii) the Crown must prove that Tremblay's pattern shows a substantial
degree of indifference in relation to the reasonably foreseeable consequences
of his persistent aggressive conduct on others and that the evidence discloses
a likelihood that such behaviour will persist in the future.

[
195
]

In assessing whether these elements are met, the
court must consider the context in which the offender committed the past
criminal conduct in order to properly assess the likelihood of that conduct
persisting in the future.

[
196
]

In my view, the length of Tremblay's pattern
(which spans a decade) and the frequency and consistency with which his
offensive conduct has occurred, clearly demonstrates a failure to restrain his
behaviour. Further, there is no indication that his controlling and assaultive
conduct is abating and there is no question that his conduct has lead to both
physical and psychological injury in some instances and the likelihood thereof
in others. Tremblay's lack of restraint is clearly evidenced by the fact that
Tremblay has committed most of the criminal conduct which makes up the pattern
while he was on probation or some form of judicial interim release. Previous
dispositions by the court have also failed to deter him from continuing his
violent criminal conduct.

[
197
]

In the result I am satisfied that, pursuant to
s. 753(1)(a)(i), Tremblay's past conduct demonstrates a likelihood that injury
or severe psychological damage may occur to others as a result of his failure
to restrain his behaviour in the future.

[
198
]

The evidence is also replete with examples of Tremblay's
persistent aggressive conduct demonstrating a substantial degree of
indifference in relation to the reasonably foreseeable consequences thereof.
His lack of remorse and consistent minimizing of his criminal conduct are
obvious examples of this indifference. His attitude in this respect was not
only testified to by his victims and the experts but was also clearly
illustrated during his own testimony at the trial of this matter and in the Beaudoin
trial. In the course of both proceedings Tremblay generally took the position
that these women were injured accidentally and that he was not to blame.
Tremblay's version of events was rejected on both occasions. This indifference
was also evidenced by the victims' testimonies which indicated Tremblay blamed
them for the beatings.

[
199
]

Based on the above considerations I am satisfied
beyond a reasonable doubt that Tremblay's aggressive, indifferent behaviour is
likely to continue. Accordingly, I am satisfied that the requirements of s.
753(1)(a)(ii) are proved.

[
200
]

In terms of context, Tremblay has victimized
roommates and women with whom he has been romantically involved. According to
Dr. Hashman's evidence, and Tremblay himself, this pattern is motivated by
insecurity. There was no suggestion that Tremblay's insecurities were motivated
by anything specific to these relationships. Thus, short of prohibiting him
from having any relationships with women, one cannot reasonably conclude that
altering the context would reduce the likelihood of future criminal conduct.

[
201
]

In relation to both of these subsections the
Crown must also show that there is a relatively high degree of intractability,
either substantially or pathologically. In other words, the reasons for the
past behaviour "should militate against any reasonable prospect for
meaningful change in the future".

[
202
]

Intractable is defined in
The
Oxford
English Dictionary,
2nd Ed. (1989) as "Not to be guided; not manageable or docile;
uncontrollable; refractory, stubborn". Dr. Hashman opined that, although
"ingrained", Tremblay's conduct is not intractable. Dr. Dutton
defined intractable as "not amenable to outside intervention by a
therapist" and concluded that Tremblay's conduct is, by that definition,
intractable.

[
203
]

In Neve the Court of Appeal noted that when an
expert opines as to an offender's intractability, realistically they must
consider an offender's treatment prospects. Certainly, Dr. Dutton's and Dr. Hashman's
respective views on treatment would explain their different opinions regarding
the intractability of Tremblay's conduct.

[
204
]

In my view, without treatment, Tremblay's
conduct demonstrates a relatively high degree of intractability. This is
evidenced by the pattern itself and confirmed in the risk assessments provided
by the experts, all of whom agreed that Tremblay is a high risk to re-offend. I
am thus satisfied that Tremblay's past conduct satisfies all of the requisite
elements of the thresholds set out at both ss. 753(1)(a)(i) and (ii).

b) The Threat Assessment

[
205
]

The next consideration prescribed in Neve is the
"threat assessment". In this regard I must find that Tremblay
constitutes a threat to the safety or physical or mental well being of others
on the basis of the evidence which established the pattern. Given that I have
already found that there is a likelihood that Tremblay will cause injury or
severe psychological harm to others in the future and that his aggressive
indifferent behaviour is likely to continue, I have no difficulty concluding
that his pattern of conduct demonstrates beyond a reasonable doubt that he
constitutes a threat for the purposes of this analysis.

[
206
]

The expert evidence serves to confirm my
conclusion. Although there were obvious disagreements amongst some of the
experts in terms of diagnosis and treatment, they all agreed that Tremblay
poses a high risk to reoffend. Given their unanimity on this point I do not
find it necessary to weigh the evidence of each expert against the other at
this stage of my analysis.

[
207
]

In finding that Tremblay represents a threat in
the future, I emphasize that my determination in that respect is made on the
basis of Tremblay's past conduct. Whether any effective form of treatment is
available and whether that consideration is of any consequence in terms of this
application will be discussed separately under the final threshold - residual
discretion.

3. If the
answers to the above questions are "yes", is a dangerous offender
designation appropriate in all of the circumstances?

[
208
]

Earlier in these reasons I held that the
residual discretion referred to in
Neve
remains despite the 1997
amendments to the
Code.

[
209
]

This final threshold was discussed by the Court
in Neve, at paragraph
229
:

"… it is at this stage of the
dangerous offender proceedings that the sentencing judge, even though satisfied
that all the statutory prerequisites have been met, should step back and
reassess the evidence having regard to this consideration: Does this offender
fall within that relatively small group of criminals in respect of whom
preventative incarceration is warranted?"

[
210
]

Declaring someone to be a dangerous offender
under our
Criminal Code

subjects an offender to the most severe
consequences known to our law save for the life sentences for murderers. Once
designated a dangerous offender, that designation remains for life. There is no
process (after exhausting the normal appeal process) for reviewing or removing
that designation. A person designated a dangerous offender must be sentenced to
imprisonment in a penitentiary for an indeterminate term. He is not entitled to
a review for parole until after he has served at least seven years. Thereafter,
he is only entitled to a parole review every two years. Drs. Weston and Baillie
testified that in their experience, dangerous offenders are given a low
priority for treatment in the penitentiary. It is reasonable to infer that lack
of treatment would negatively affect a dangerous offender's chance of being
granted parole.

[
211
]

Exhibit S-50, a report on Dangerous Offenders In
Canada prepared by Elizabeth Baylis of Corrections Canada and dated January 31, 2000 states that there are currently
248 dangerous offenders under federal jurisdiction serving indeterminate
sentences. Of these 248, 243 are incarcerated in federal institutions, four are
in the community on conditional release, and one has been deported. Ignoring the
one deported, these statistics indicate that of those currently serving
indeterminate sentences as dangerous offenders, only 1.6 % have been allowed
back into the community on conditional release. Practically speaking,
therefore, designating someone a dangerous offender may very well have the
effect of sentencing that person to a life of imprisonment.

[
212
]

In Neve, the Court identified three matters
which should be considered in this final step: the relative degree of
seriousness of the criminal conduct and the extent of the offender's moral
blameworthiness; treatment prospects; and the offender him or herself.

(a) Relative Degree of the Seriousness of the
Criminal Conduct and Moral Blameworthiness

[
213
]

The most serious offence for which Tremblay has
ever been convicted is assault causing bodily harm. In terms of the relative
degree of seriousness of criminal conduct, assault causing bodily harm does not
rank as one of the most serious offences in the
Criminal Code
.

[
214
]

Tremblay has never received a penitentiary term
of imprisonment. The longest sentence which he has received to date is six
months. I note that he was sentenced to a custodial term of one year but that
sentence was reduced to six months on appeal. This indicates that the judges
who have previously sentenced Tremblay were not of the view that his previous
offences warranted a term of federal incarceration. A similar observation was
made by our Court of Appeal in
Neve
.

[
215
]

There is no indication that the nature of
Tremblay's conduct will become more dangerous in the future. Dr. Nesca's
evidence was that Tremblay demonstrates a clear persistent pattern. He was
unable to predict an escalation in Tremblay's conduct other than to say that
the assaultive behaviour is occurring earlier in the relationships. Dr. Dutton
testified that individuals suffering from mixed personality disorders are an
extremely high risk to continue to do what they have been doing. Dr. Hashman
described Tremblay as a high risk to reoffend in a similar manner. Thus it
appears that although Tremblay is a high risk to continue to commit the same
types of offences, there is no evidence that the severity of his conduct will
increase.

[
216
]

Having said that, I acknowledge that his most
recent offences, those perpetrated against Monilaws, were the most injurious.
However, in Monilaws' case the nature and quality of the conduct was not
significantly different than that which he has demonstrated throughout the life
of his pattern.

[
217
]

In terms of the injurious nature of an
offender's conduct, the Court in
Neve
stated, at paragraph
279
:

"… the fact that the offences which Neve
committed did not, with two exceptions (the two assaults), result in serious
injuries to anyone is a weighty factor militating against designating Neve a
dangerous offender. And in evaluating the relative seriousness of the injuries
resulting from the two assaults, we note that in neither of the two cases were
the injuries life-threatening or permanent."

[
218
]

The current case is not a strict parallel in the
sense that there is some suggestion that the injury to Monilaws' thumb may be
permanent. Nonetheless, although there is no question that these women have
suffered a great deal as a result of Tremblay's criminal conduct, I am obliged
to consider that conduct in the context of criminal conduct generally. Against
that backdrop, and in comparison specifically to other offenders and offences
in previous dangerous offender applications, I cannot conclude that Tremblay's
conduct is at the most severe end of the spectrum. Having said that, I am
mindful that the backdrop can be expanded in terms of offences or offenders, as
was noted by the Court in
Neve
.

[
219
]

In concluding that Tremblay's conduct,
relatively speaking, is not at the most severe end of the spectrum, I have of
course considered the psychological evidence presented regarding the effect
that Tremblay's conduct has had on his victims, particularly Hallson and Monilaws.
I must comment that I found the evidence in that regard to be less than
satisfactory. Given that both Hallson and Monilaws have apparently been treated
for the psychological consequences that they have suffered as a result of their
victimization by Tremblay, I would have expected to hear evidence from their
respective physicians and/or therapists. I am also of the view that having a
representative from the Crown's office present and participating during the
interviews with Dr. Dutton made the resulting evidence less reliable than it
might have been. Specifically, I have concerns that the interviewees may have
felt pressured to answer questions in a particular way because of the presence
and participation of the Crown. Due to the lack of reliable evidence regarding
the degree of psychological harm that those women suffered, I cannot
characterize it as severe.

[
220
]

Tremblay's offences are not of the kind
typically seen in relation to a dangerous offender application. For example in
the recent decision in
R. v. L.C.W.,

2000 SKQB 302 (CanLII)
, [2000] S.J. No. 422; 195 Sask.R. 1
(Q.B.), the offender's previous criminal record included rape, assault and
aggravated sexual assault. The predicate offence in that case was sexual
assault causing bodily harm against a 75 year old woman in ill health. There
the offender broke into her house found her laying on her bed using her
ventilator. He sat down on the bed and announced that he was going to rape her.
He smashed her ventilator mask and continued to strike her in the face with his
fists. He pulled off her pants and continued striking her in the face, head,
shoulders and arms. While the offender was masturbating, the victim activated her
life monitoring system which scared him off. The offender in that case was
designated as a dangerous offender.

[
221
]

In
R. v. J.Y.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 4916 (SK CA)
, 141 Sask.R. 132;

114 W.A.C. 132
; 104 C.C.C.(3d) 512 (C.A.), the offender was convicted of: three
counts of having sexual intercourse with a girl under the age of 14; two counts
of having sexual intercourse with a woman without her consent; assault; assault
causing bodily harm; buggery; an act of bestiality; rape; and two counts of
indecent assault. He was designated as a dangerous offender.

[
222
]

In
R. v. McArthur (M.)
(1998), 77 O.T.C.
119 (Gen. Div.)
, the offender was convicted of an extensive list of serious
personal injury offences that arose from a bank robbery, including; four counts
of attempted murder; one count of aggravated assault; one count of robbery;
three counts of using a firearm in the commission of an offence; two counts of
possessing a weapon; two counts of being disguised with intent; one count of
possessing a prohibited weapon; one count of forcible confinement; one count of
kidnapping; and one count of breaking and entering with intent. While
acknowledging the gravity of the offences, the trial judge was unable to find
that the offender met the necessary threshold to be labelled a dangerous
offender.

[
223
]

In
R. v. Imming,
1999 CanLII 12054 (QC CS)
, [2000] R.J.Q. 215
(S.C.), the offender who was ultimately designated a dangerous offender, was
convicted of assault with a weapon, assault causing bodily harm, threats and
sexual assault all against his common law wife. His pattern included previous
convictions for assault and assault with a weapon also against his common Jaw
wife. Additionally, he had been convicted of extremely assaultive conduct in
relation to his former wife. That conduct involved a particularly severe
beating with a tire iron which left her with permanent imprints on her body,
poor vision and an inability to perform mathematical functions. She had to have
77% of her liver removed and would have to undergo a liver transplant within
five years. She had great difficulty walking and had to use a cane. She was
also unable to hold a job as a result of the assault.

[
224
]

Tremblay has not been charged with aggravated
assault, attempted murder or sexual assault, let al.one convicted of such
offences. As a result of the offences he has committed no one was killed, no
one was tortured, no one was sexually assaulted, and no one received any life
threatening injuries. In fact, it has never been suggested that Tremblay has
demonstrated or will in the future demonstrate that degree of violence.

[
225
]

This is not to say that violence in a domestic
context will never support a dangerous offender designation. In fact the courts
have, on at least two occasions, made a dangerous offender designation in the
context of domestic violence. I am specifically referring to the decisions in
R.
v. Imming
,
supra, and
R. v. Gaudry (R.E.)
(1996),
1996 CanLII 19913 (AB PC)
, 186 A.R. 91 (Prov.
Ct.), affd. (1998),
1998 ABCA 18 (CanLII)
, 212 A.R. 39;
168 W.A.C. 39 (C.A.)
. In those decisions, however, the injuries and the violence were
much more severe than is the case here.

[
226
]

I recognize that had it been Parliament's
intention to designate as dangerous only those offenders who had perpetrated
the most brutal offences, it would have limited the applicable threshold to s.
753(1)(a)(iii). Instead it has seen fit to provide for the designation of
offenders who qualify under s. 753(1)(a)(i) and (ii).

[
227
]

Nonetheless, I must be mindful of, and I am of
course bound by, the Court of Appeal's repeated remarks in
Neve
that the
dangerous offender legislation is intended to catch only a small group of
highly dangerous criminals. In that regard the Court stated, at paragraph 59:

"Not everyone who is a criminal or
for that matter a danger to the public is a dangerous offender. In the spectrum
of offenders, the dangerous offender legislation is designed to target - and -
capture those clustered at or near the extreme end. Were this otherwise,
constitutionality might stumble. In other words, the dangerous offender
legislation is not intended to be a process of general application but rather
of exacting selection."

[
228
]

In the result, I cannot find that Tremblay falls
within that small group. Without minimizing Tremblay's abhorrent conduct, in a
relative sense it cannot in my view be considered "at or near the extreme
end".

[
229
]

In terms of Tremblay's moral blameworthiness,
there was some suggestion by Dr. Weston that Tremblay's early childhood,
specifically, living in a number of different homes, was to blame for some of
his conduct. The evidence given by Tremblay's mother indicates that his
childhood was less than ideal. However, that factor does not, in my view,
significantly diminish his moral blameworthiness.

(b) Treatment Prospects

[
230
]

In my view Tremblay's treatment prospects also
dictate against designating him a dangerous offender. Those prospects will be
dealt with more fully below as part of the long-term offender analysis.

(c) The Offender Himself

[
231
]

I accept Dr. Hashman's evidence that Tremblay
has not been given an opportunity to receive intensive, long-term treatment.
First, the two attempts that Tremblay has made to obtain treatment on his own
were terminated as a result of circumstances beyond his control. On the one
occasion that he pursued treatment while he was incarcerated he was moved into
segregation which made it impossible for him to continue. When he began
counselling while living with the Nissens his counsellor moved out of town.

[
232
]

Second, on only one occasion was treatment ever
included as a probation condition despite the obvious pattern of offences
against women which had been occurring for almost seven years when he received
his last sentence. Even more remarkable is the fact that on that one occasion
when treatment was imposed as a probation condition, Tremblay failed to comply
and no consequences followed as a result.

[
233
]

We do not know what the outcome might have been
if Tremblay had been subjected to more rigorous treatment conditions and the
appropriate authorities had made more of an effort to ensure compliance. That
has not yet been tried. Certainly, where there is a reasonable possibility of
controlling the offender's conduct within the community, more of an effort
ought to be made in that direction prior to resorting to the most serious penal
consequence known to Canadian criminal law, short of a life sentence.

CONCLUSION

[
234
]

As was stated by the court in
Neve
,
at
paragraph
290
:

"There is no doubt that Neve has a
history of offending the law; and we cannot say that Neve will not re-offend.
That risk exists and it is a real risk. Indeed it would be naive to think
otherwise. However, the question is not whether there is a possibility or even
a probability of Neve's reoffending in the future. While this consideration
certainly goes on the scale the central question which must be addressed at
this stage is whether given her past record and the various factors that we
have noted and assessed, Neve falls within the intended small group of
offenders in Canada. In our
view she does not."

[
235
]

In my view these comments apply with equal force
to Tremblay. I decline to designate him as a dangerous offender.

4. If a dangerous
offender designation is inappropriate should Tremblay be designated as a
long-term offender in accordance with s. 753.1?

[
236
]

Having declined to designate Tremblay as a
dangerous offender under s. 753, I must now consider whether Tremblay ought to
be designated as a long-term offender pursuant to s. 753.1. The long-term
offender designation entails the imposition of a definite sentence of
imprisonment followed by a long-term community supervision order.

[
237
]

Section 753.1
of the
Criminal Code

states
that the court may find an offender to be a long-term offender if it is
satisfied that:

"(a) it would be appropriate to
impose a sentence of imprisonment of two years or more for the offence for
which the offender has been convicted;

"(b) there is a substantial risk that
the offender will re-offend; and

"(c) there is a reasonable
possibility of eventual control of the risk in the community."

[
238
]

I am satisfied that Tremblay's conviction for
assault causing bodily harm in relation to Monilaws is deserving of a sentence
of imprisonment of more than two years.

[
239
]

The psychiatrists and psychologists who
testified were unanimous in their opinion that Tremblay poses a serious risk to
re-offend. In my analysis of whether Tremblay qualifies for the dangerous
offender designation, I found that he satisfied both of the thresholds under s.
753(1)(a)(i) and (ii) and that he constitutes a threat to the safety and
physical and mental well being of others. Based on that evidence and analysis I
am satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Tremblay satisfies the second
prerequisite under
s. 753.1
in that there is a substantial risk that he will
re-offend.

[
240
]

There remains to be considered whether there is
a "reasonable possibility" of eventually controlling the risk
Tremblay poses in the community.

[
241
]

The experts did not entirely agree on Tremblay's
diagnosis. However, of the five mental health experts called to give evidence,
only Dr. Hashman diagnosed Tremblay as something other than a psychopath.
Instead, Dr. Hashman said that Tremblay suffers from a mixed personality
disorder. He explained that he did not administer the PCL-R to Tremblay.
Rather, he chose to use more standardized diagnostic labels from the DSM. Psychopathy,
according to Dr. Hashman, is "just another paradigm". When asked
whether his diagnosis indicates that Tremblay is not a psychopath, he replied
"not at all". Dr. Nesca also testified that psychopathy and
antisocial, borderline, narcissistic, paranoid type personality disorders are
really the same thing. This testimony, together with my evaluation of the
various opinions and my consequential findings, makes it unnecessary for me to
make a finding that Tremblay is a psychopath for the purpose of evaluating his
treatment prospects.

[
242
]

In addition to their disagreement in terms of
diagnosis the experts also provided a number of different views in relation to
Tremblay's treatment prospects. Dr. Weston testified that Tremblay is
treatable. Dr. Hashman also testified that there was a reasonable possibility
of successful treatment and both he and Dr. Weston suggested that the most
appropriate place for Tremblay to receive treatment is at the ABC Program at
the RPC in Saskatoon. Drs.
Dutton and Nesca felt that regardless of whether Tremblay suffered from psychopathy
or personality disorders there was no possibility of successful treatment. In
fact, they commented that if Tremblay is a psychopath, treatment may have a
negative effect in the sense that it might make him a better psychopath. Dr.
Baillie agreed with Drs. Weston and Hashman to the extent that he thought that
Tremblay would benefit from treatment. However, Dr. Baillie believed that the
ABC Program would be inappropriate and that the treatment set out in the
Program Guidelines for the Institutional Treatment of Violent Psychopaths, currently
being developed by Drs. Hare and West, would be the most beneficial to
Tremblay.

[
243
]

In terms of weighing the evidence given by the
various experts, I begin by noting that all of the experts who were called
during the course of this application were eminently qualified to give opinion
evidence.

[
244
]

In terms of evaluating one opinion in relation
to another I must consider the fact that Dr. Dutton did not interview Tremblay.
Although this may not have effected the results of the PCL-R, I cannot give his
opinion the same weight as I might have had an interview been conducted. As set
out at paragraph 190 of
Neve:

"The court must be interested
primarily in each psychiatrists assessment of the person under scrutiny. That
is not to say that secondary sources, documents, discussions with third parties
are not valid and important for the psychiatrist to review. However, taking the
offender out of the psychiatrist - patient relationship may leave the
psychiatrist in the role of interpreter only."

[
245
]

And later, at paragraph 195:

"Another consideration which
potentially affects the weight of expert evidence has to do with the expert's
contact with the offender."

[
246
]

Additionally, Dr. Dutton did not review
Tremblay's testimony at trial which, in my view, makes the database upon which
he based his opinion even more unreliable.

[
247
]

Finally, I cannot ignore the fact that Dr.
Dutton was called as a Crown witness at the trial of this matter. That factor
leads me to believe that Dr. Dutton may have been less than entirely objective
in assessing Tremblay in relation to the present application.

[
248
]

With respect to Dr. Nesca's evidence I must take
into account the obvious lack of rapport, if not open hostility, between him
and Tremblay during the one attempted interview. I am mindful of the fact that
the Court in
Neve
found that generally, courts should not be too quick
to reject the evidence of an expert, particularly a Crown expert, in instances
where the offender has refused to cooperate. Nonetheless, I cannot ignore the
obvious conflict which developed between the two or the fact that Tremblay
terminated the interview after only one and three-quarter hours. I would also
note that in this case, Tremblay participated in approximately 10 hours of
interviews with Dr. Hashman thereby indicating a conflict between Dr. Nesca and
Tremblay rather than a general unwillingness to cooperate on Tremblay's part.

[
249
]

I have some concern with Dr. Weston's evidence
as it appeared after cross-examination that he was unsure of the material he
had reviewed and he did not know the extent of Tremblay's criminal record. I
note also that he revised his initial risk assessment of Tremblay during
cross-examination. These factors have negatively influenced the weight I am
prepared to give his evidence.

[
250
]

Dr. Hashman spent over 10 hours interviewing
Tremblay and caused three separate tests to be administered to Tremblay, the
results of which Dr. Hashman then analysed prior to making his findings. He
reviewed all of the relevant material and his opinions remained unshaken during
cross-examination. He also appeared to be objective in the sense that his
evidence was neither entirely in favour of the Crown nor the Defence.

[
251
]

Dr. Baillie's testimony also impressed me as
being objective. He too was unshaken during cross examination. He also appeared
to have a very firm grasp of the evidence called both at trial and during this
application.

[
252
]

Without ignoring the evidence of Drs. Nesca,
Weston and Dutton, I was most impressed with the evidence provided by Drs. Hashman
and Baillie. As a consequence, I have given their evidence the most weight.

[
253
]

To summarize, Dr. Hashman recommended that
Tremblay receive very intensive, long-term treatment and that he attend at the
ABC Program which is available to individuals within the penitentiary system.
That program, according to Dr. Hashman, involves a variety of therapies
including group and individual therapy and a domestic violence group which
challenges the offender's belief system which underlies his or her controlling
and abusive behaviour. Dr. Hashman explained that this program is geared
towards individuals who have significant personality disorders.

[
254
]

Dr. Hashman suggested that Tremblay is currently
facing a "reality check" in the sense that these proceeding have
demonstrated to him that if he does not take advantage of treatment he will
likely destroy the rest of his life. Dr. Hashman indicated that a sincere
desire to receive treatment is necessary in order to achieve any success and
although he could not predict whether Tremblay would take advantage of it, Dr. Hashman
felt that Tremblay should be afforded an opportunity to receive more than the
"minor" treatment attempted to date.

[
255
]

Ultimately, he concluded that there is a
"reasonable chance"that Tremblay will benefit from treatment.

[
256
]

Dr. Baillie diagnosed Tremblay as a psychopath
and stated that there is a small opportunity that Tremblay would benefit from
treatment if it was "prolonged, regular and competently provided and [he]
is effectively engaged with his therapist and avoiding all forms of significant
heterosexual relationships". According to Dr. Baillie a large part of
treating Tremblay would involve controlling external factors, most importantly
that Tremblay be prevented from being involved in any non-employment type
relationships with women.

[
257
]

In Dr. Baillie's opinion, psychopathic offenders
do not respond well to attempts at altering their feelings towards their
victims, or changing their personalities. Rather, Dr. Baillie believes that
competent treatment for psychopaths requires a relapse prevention model of
treatment; one that appeals to the rational self-interest of the offender in
order to change his behaviour. According to Dr. Baillie this is the basis of
the program currently being developed by Drs. Hare and Wong.

[
258
]

Dr. Baillie testified that the fundamental issue
regarding treatment of Tremblay is whether he is willing to comply when it is
in his self-interest to do so. Dr. Baillie viewed that as a distinct
possibility. He testified that Tremblay has recognized that his behaviour is a
problem and that he has acknowledged that the problems essentially start with
him. Further, he testified that he was satisfied that Tremblay can comply with
any condition applied to him if he wants to. Dr. Baillie said that he has
already seen a degree of motivation to change in Tremblay.

[
259
]

Dr. Baillie defined "treatment" to
include the control of external factors. Obviously any such control could be
accommodated by the long-term supervision order available through a long-term
offender designation.

[
260
]

In terms of the evidence given by the other
experts in this respect, Dr. Weston also felt that Tremblay was treatable and
that he might benefit from the ABC program. Thus, both of the psychiatrists who
gave evidence felt that Tremblay could benefit from treatment.

[
261
]

Dr. Weston also gave evidence of a burn-out
theory, which essentially predicts psychopaths become less violent at or about
the age of 40. Without giving too much credence to this theory, the imposition
of a significant penitentiary term together with a long-term supervision order,
may ensure that Tremblay is supervised in the community until such time as he
is less likely to behave in a criminal or violent manner.

[
262
]

Further, this is not a case where treatment has
failed in the past. As set out earlier in this Judgment there have not yet been
any real attempts to control Tremblay in the community through treatment or
through sincere efforts at supervision.

[
263
]

Section 753.1 requires only that there be a
reasonable
possibility
of
eventually
controlling the risk that Tremblay poses in
the community. The section does not require a certainty, or even a probability.
It does not require that an offender be "cured" so long as the risk
he or she poses can be controlled. Based on the evidence presented by the
experts regarding treatment, I find that a reasonable possibility does exist
that the risk Tremblay poses in the community can be controlled. Paragraph (c)
of
s. 753.1
is therefore satisfied.

[
264
]

It follows that the three pre-requisites under

s. 753.1
have been proved beyond a reasonable doubt. I am satisfied that it is
necessary, desirable and in the interests of the public that Tremblay be
declared to be a long-term offender and I therefore make that finding.

SENTENCING

[
265
]

Accordingly, I must now determine the
appropriate sentence for Tremblay with respect to the six charges of which I
have convicted him. In determining the appropriate sentences, I have instructed
myself in accordance with the relevant provisions of the
Criminal Code

including

ss. 718
,
718.1
and
718.2
.

[
266
]

Section 753.1(3)
of the
Criminal Code

provides
that if the court finds the offender to be a long-term offender, it shall

"(a) impose a sentence for the
offence for which the offender has been convicted, which sentence must be a
minimum punishment of imprisonment for a term of two years; and

"(b) order the offender to be
supervised in the community, for a period not exceeding ten years, in
accordance with s. 753.2 and the
Corrections and Conditional Release Act
."

[
267
]

Paragraph (a) of s. 753.1(3) refers to the
predicate offence. In Tremblay's case, this is the conviction for assault
causing bodily harm in relation to Monilaws. The assault on Monilaws
encompassed over twenty incidents of violence, some of which took place in
front of Monilaws' two year old son, and much of which involved choking. This
assault is aggravated by the fact that it was spousal violence as Tremblay and Monilaws
were living together at the time. I am influenced by the lack of remorse
exhibited by Tremblay and the ease with which he blames his victims for his
criminal behaviour. The fact that he commits assaults primarily against women
is aggravating in my view. I am also mindful of the fact that on three previous
separate occasions he has been sentenced to six months' incarceration for
assaulting women.

[
268
]

There are no mitigating factors in this case
other than the time Tremblay has served since conviction and I will deal with
that later in this Judgment.

[
269
]

The courts view domestic abuse very seriously. I
agree with and adopt the recent comments of the Ontario Court of Appeal in
R.
v. Bates (D.R.),

2000 CanLII 5759 (ON CA)
, [2000] O.J. No. 2558; 134 O.A.C. 156 (C.A.), at paragraph 30:

"Crimes involving abuse in domestic
relationships are particularly heinous because they are not isolated events in
the life of the victim. Rather, the victim is often subjected not only to
continuing abuse, both physical and emotional, but also experiences perpetual
fear of the offender."

[
270
]

Tremblay's assault on Monilaws was cowardly,
inexcusable, unacceptable and intolerable. It warrants a severe sentence of
imprisonment. Therefore, in the interests of protecting the public, denouncing
and deterring such crimes, and in order to persuade Tremblay to change his
behaviour, I sentence him to four years imprisonment for the assault causing
bodily harm.

[
271
]

In addition to the assault causing bodily harm,
Tremblay was also convicted of unlawful confinement and criminal harassment in
relation to Monilaws. For these offences, I am imposing a global sentence of
two years to be served concurrently with the sentence for assault causing bodily
harm. I have considered the almost constant terror Tremblay visited upon Monilaws
and how, on at least one occasion, the unlawful confinement prolonged the
duration of an assault and contributed to his victim's sense of helplessness
and fear.

[
272
]

In relation to Hallson, Tremblay was convicted
of assault, unlawful confinement and uttering threats. For these offences,
which I perceive to be less severe than those perpetrated against Monilaws yet
equally intolerable and abhorrent, I am imposing a global sentence of one and
one-half years. However, because these offences took place at a separate time
and relate to a separate victim, this sentence is to be served consecutively
with the four years imposed for the crimes against Monilaws. In the result, I
am imposing a sentence of five and one-half years in respect of these six
convictions.

[
273
]

The Crown asks that I make an order under s.
743.6(1) requiring that Tremblay serve one-half of his sentence before becoming
eligible to be released on full parole.

[
274
]

In
R. v. Matwiy (S.B.) and Langston (J.D.)
(1996),

1996 ABCA 63 (CanLII)
, 178 A.R. 356; 110 W.A.C. 356; 105 C.C.C.(3d) 251 (C.A.), the Alberta Court
of Appeal held, at page 268 [C.C.C.]:

"As a general rule an order under s.
741.2 [now s. 743.6(1)] increasing parole ineligibility should not be made.
However, where the trial judge is satisfied, having regard to the circumstances
of the offence and the circumstances and character of the accused, that the
objectives of the expression of society's denunciation or specific or general
deterrence so require, the judge may make the order increasing parole
ineligibility.

. . . . .

"The judge, having determined the
appropriate or fit term of imprisonment, may make the s. 741.2 order [now s.
743.6] only if convinced that the objectives of the expression of society's
denunciation or specific or general deterrence will not be met unless the
possibility of early release on full parole is barred. In other words, that the
term of imprisonment alone is insufficient to accomplish those objectives, or
any one of them. That decision must be based on the circumstances of the
offence and the character and circumstances of the offender or a combination of
these factors. The factor of the character of the offender and his
circumstances, of necessity includes an assessment of the possibility of the
rehabilitation or, more accurately, the unlikelihood of rehabilitation within
the regular period of parole ineligibility, and the need to protect society by
the incapacitation of the offender for a longer period than would normally
occur, given the sentence imposed and the rules regarding the granting of
parole."

[
275
]

In Tremblay's case I am satisfied that an order
should be made under s. 743.6 as requested by the Crown, for the following
reasons. First, these offences were committed by Tremblay while he was on some
form of probation or judicial release.

[
276
]

Second, it was clear to me from the evidence of
those experts who expressed the opinion that Tremblay would benefit from
treatment, that they believed a significant period of incarceration was
required - both to deter Tremblay from repeating his criminal behaviour as well
as to provide ample time for Tremblay to receive treatment in the institution,
such as the ABC program previously mentioned. For example, Dr. Weston opined
that a lot of work needed to be done with Tremblay and that was why he appeared
to favour a long but not indefinite period of incarceration. Dr. Baillie viewed
incarceration itself to be a form of treatment. Dr. Hashman recommended that
Tremblay receive "very intensive long-term treatment" in a controlled
setting such as the ABC Program at Corrections Canada's Regional Psychiatric
Centre.

[
277
]

Consequently, I am convinced that the objectives
of specific and general deterrence will not be met unless the possibility of early
release on full parole is barred and therefore I make an order under s.
743.6(1).

[
278
]

The defence submits that Tremblay ought to be
given credit for the time he has served in remand since March 24, 1999. I am
not prepared to accede to this request. Tremblay was remanded in custody
because he committed the Monilaws offences while he was on release in relation
to the Hallson offences. Thus, he has been the author of his own misfortune in
terms of the time that he has spent in custody awaiting his trial.

[
279
]

I do, however, think it is appropriate to give
Tremblay credit for the time he has spent in custody since his conviction
awaiting the conclusion of this application - a period of seven months, and I
so order. In the result, applying seven months credit to the five and one-half
year sentence results in a net sentence remaining of four years and eleven
months.

[
280
]

Paragraph (b) of s. 753.1(3) provides for the
imposition of a long-term supervision order. Though I believe that there is
reasonable possibility of eventually controlling the risk that Tremblay poses
to the community, I am also of the opinion that Tremblay requires strict
supervision for a long time to come. For that reason, I am ordering that
Tremblay be supervised in the community for the maximum ten year period.

[
281
]

The
Corrections and Conditional Release Act,
S.C.
1992, c. 20, s. 134.1(1) as am. by S.C. 1997, C. 17, s. 30 provides for the
inclusion of a standard set of terms in long-term supervision orders.
Additional terms may be added on a case-by-case basis by the National Parole
Board pursuant to s. 134.1(2) of the
Act.
Adopting an advisory role, I
strongly urge the National Parole Board to consider the following conditions
for inclusion in Tremblay's long-term supervision order:

1. That Tremblay be
prohibited from contacting any of the victims or their families;

2. That Tremblay be
prohibited from entering into any kind of a relationship with any woman without
the knowledge and consent of his parole officer;

3. That Tremblay be
prohibited from living in a house or apartment with any woman, without the
express knowledge and consent of his parole officer;

4. That Tremblay be
prohibited from changing his name or using an alias and that he must at all
times identify himself by the name "Jean Guy Tremblay";

5. That Tremblay take
and complete such courses and treatment as his parole officer may direct;

I further recommend that Tremblay's parole
officer make unannounced evening inspections to Tremblay's residence in the
community to ensure that he is complying with his parole conditions.

[
282
]

The Crown has made an application on behalf of Monilaws
for a restitution order in the amount of $26,799.41, pursuant to s. 738. To
date she has received $10,750 from the Crimes Compensation Board - $8,750 for
emotional harm, $1,250 for the injuries to her thumb and $1,000 for other
injuries.

[
283
]

The only evidence tendered which relates
directly in relation to the losses for which Monilaws seeks compensation was in
the form of a schedule and a bundle of receipts which was submitted during the
Crown's closing argument. The losses for which she seeks compensation include,
among other things, the cost of new prescription glasses due to a change of
prescription, unnecessary legal expenses in relation to custody and access
matters regarding her son and loss of funds which she says resulted from the
sale of her house and car. These claims appear to be more in the nature of
damages than restitution. Accordingly, the proper forum for determining these
issues is a civil court and it is not, in my view, appropriate to deal with
them in these proceedings.

CONCLUSION

[
284
]

To summarize:

(1) the Crown's
application under s. 753(1) to have Tremblay declared a dangerous offender is
dismissed;

(2) the Crown's
alternative application under s. 753.1(1) to have Tremblay declared a long-term

an order under
s. 753.1(3)
requiring that Tremblay be supervised in the
community for a period of 10 years after his release from penitentiary;

sentenced to four years in respect of the Monilaws offences and one and
